title.en: Starkadr: The Giant-Kin Champion Cursed by Both Gods
title.zh: 斯塔卡德：被雙神愛恨交織的巨人族戰士

region.en: Vidgota-land and the Baltic coast (symbolic pin at Västergötland, Sweden)
region.zh: 維德戈塔蘭與波羅的海沿岸（象徵性定位於瑞典西約特蘭）

texts.period: Gautreks saga 14th century (older heroic material); Saxo Grammaticus, Gesta Danorum book 6-8 (c. 1200); also Vikarsbalki verse

source.work: Gautreks saga (Vikar chapter); Saxo, Gesta Danorum book 6 (Starkather); English: Gautrek's Saga, trans. Pálsson & Edwards 1970; Saxo trans. Elton 1894

texts.license: Public domain (Elton 1894); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Starkadr is the grandson of a giant and the strongest man of his age - and the corpus's most doubled fate. Odin, visiting the boat in disguise, blesses him with eight lifetimes of victory, the choicest arms, the poet's fame - and Thor, the other passenger, curses each blessing: shall he never win a fight outright? shall he have no children, the vilest of deeds done by his hand, the sorest of wounds always? shall he be hung from his own arms? shall he know no rest in age? shall he forget his deeds? shall his life be a crime's exile? - the gods divide him: Odin's gifts are all diluted by Thor's clauses. And the life delivers: victory without joy, patricide? - the sacrifice of King Vikar by his own hand on Odin's tree, the nine-year? - the record is the champion as a treaty-object between two gods who will not share him.
summary.zh: 斯塔卡德是巨人之孫、其時代最強者——也是語料中命運最撕裂的英雄。奧丁喬裝登船，賜予他八個生命週期的勝利、最精良的兵刃與詩人的名聲；而同船的索爾逐項加以詛咒：願他從未完勝一戰；願他無後，親手犯下最卑劣之事，傷痛永續；願他被倒吊；願他老無安寧；願他忘卻榮光；願其生涯以流放罪行終結。兩神分割了他：奧丁的每一項恩賜，都被索爾的條款所稀釋。而他的一生恰如所願：勝而無歡，親手在奧丁之樹上獻祭維卡爾王……此記錄刻畫的是一位被兩位互不相讓的神瓜分為「條約對象」的戰士。

texts.canonical_translation: Hermann Pálsson and Paul Edwards, Gautrek's Saga, London 1970; Saxo trans. Oliver Elton 1894 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Starkadr's biography is distributed across three sources - Gautreks saga's Vikar-chapter, Saxo's Starkather-books, and the eddic-adjacent Vikarsbalki - and all three agree on the myth's structure: a champion shared between two gods on opposite terms. The blessing-scene: the old man Starkadr, back from Uppsala with his father? - the frame: young Starkadr? - Gautreks saga's version: on the boat crossing to the king Vikar, two passengers are taken aboard - an old man in a hood (Odin) and another; in the night the old man wakes the ship, and the blessing-ritual begins: 'I lay this blessing? - the verse: Odin says 'you shall be blessed? - the gifts: life eight times? - the blessing: 'thou shalt have victory in every fight? - life for the span of eight men? - the arms and riches of the best; the poet's fame; the chiefest? - and after each clause, the other god (Thor, unnamed but pointed as the hater) lays a curse: 'thou shalt do a deed of shame each? - 'thou shalt never win a victory but that thou? - 'thou shalt not have children'; 'thou shalt never have? - 'thou shalt be wounded sore? - 'thou shalt live long? - and be hung? - 'thou shalt not remember? - 'thou shalt never? - rest; the famous clauses: 'thou shalt commit the vilest of deeds? - 'and be hung from thine own? - arms'; 'thou shalt not live? - in peace; 'thou shalt have a life of exile'; and the clause on the arms: 'a horse's skull? - the arms? - shall come from the horse's? - the poisoned? - gift of arms that kills him.

The life delivers the mixture. Starkadr's fame is real - Saxo's Brávellir-battle champion, the slayer of twelve? - the terror of the age; his shame is real - the Vikar-sacrifice: stranded by winds, the fleet casts lots for a man to hang for Odin; the lot falls on King Vikar; Starkadr, the king's own champion, is coached by Odin (in the old man's shape) how to do it 'so that it be not? - a real hanging? - the apparatus: a sprig of hart's-tongue? - the mock-tree, a pig-gut for the rope, a reed for the spear - and Starkadr says 'now I give thee to Odin'? - and the reed becomes a spear and the gut a rope and the bough a tree: the mock-hanging is real by the god's engineering; and Starkadr's hand has done 'the vilest of deeds' - the king's death at his own? - champion's hand. The age: he lives on - the eighth-life? - 'he was so old that? - no man remembered his deeds? - the forgetting-clause; and his death, in the saga: 'he? - his neck? - he was struck? - the hanging-from-own-arms fulfilled.

The record's cultural functions are the treaty-champion doctrine and the double-bookkeeping of fame. The blessing-curse scene is the myth corpus's most precise portrait of what divine favor costs: each gift has a rider, and the rider is another god's signature - the champion is the treaty-object between Odin (who wants the sacrifice, the fame, the arms) and Thor (who hates the giant-kin and taxes every gift). And the Vikar-sacrifice is the corpus's most explicit myth-of-ritual: a real hanging staged as a mock-hanging by divine equipment - the doctrine that ritual's props (bark, gut, reed) are real when the god speaks the words. In the atlas, the record anchors the god-divided-champion family (the Greek Heracles' mixed parentage-curses, the Irish Cuchulainn's geasa): each a hero bound by divine contracts in opposite directions.

functions: Treaty-champion doctrine: the hero as an object divided between two gods on opposite terms
Blessing-with-rider structure: every gift taxed by the rival god's clause
Ritual-engineering doctrine: mock-hanging made real by divine props
Forgetting-clause: fame that outlives its own memory

title.en: The Battle of Brávellir: Odin Harvests Two Armies
title.zh: 布拉瓦利爾會戰：奧丁收割兩軍

region.zh: 瑞典東約特蘭布拉瓦利爾平原

texts.period: Saxo, Gesta Danorum book 7 (c. 1200); Sogubrot af nokkrum fornkonungum (late legendary saga); skaldic echoes in Eiriksmal-tradition

source.work: Saxo, Gesta Danorum book 7 (Harald and Sigurd Ring); Sogubrot af nokkrum fornkonungum; English: Elton 1894

texts.license: Public domain (Elton 1894); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Harald Wartooth, king of Denmark, grown old and famous, hears that his nephew's vassal Sigurd Ring rules Sweden without asking leave, and declares war so that he may die in battle rather than of age - the doctrine he states plainly: 'it is better to die with glory than to rot? - 'the old? - an old man's death-bed? - 'glory's death is better than the bed's'. The armies meet at Brávellir in the greatest battle the north remembers: seven days of ordered slaughter, Starkadr on both sides, ring-giving kings, and Odin's farmhand? - the god present in disguise as the one-eyed charioteer Bruni? - driving Harald's chariot straight into a pile? - the god harvests both armies: Harald dies by Odin's own club thrown from the chariot? - the ring-giver's death; and the field, littered with kings and champions, becomes the myth-image of Valhalla's recruitment: the battle is a levy for Ragnarok, fought to supply the einherjar.
summary.zh: 丹麥王哈拉爾·戰牙垂垂老矣、功名赫赫，聽聞侄兒的封臣西格德·林未經請示便統治瑞典，遂宣戰——他親口道出其志：寧以榮光赴死，不願老朽於床榻。兩軍會戰於布拉瓦利爾平原，規模冠絕北方記憶：七日有秩序的屠殺，斯塔卡德先後效力兩方，散金贈劍的諸王……而喬裝成獨眼御者「布魯尼」的奧丁親自驅動哈拉爾的戰車直衝敵陣——神明收割兩軍：哈拉爾死於奧丁親擲的戰棒之下；戰場上王者與勇士橫陳，成為瓦爾哈拉徵兵的神話意象——這場大戰正是為諸神黃昏大軍而設的徵集。

texts.canonical_translation: Oliver Elton, The First Nine Books of the Danish History, London 1894 (public domain); Sogubrot per Fornaldar sogur ed. Rafn

narrative.en:
The battle of Brávellir is the legendary Sweden-Denmark war-cycle's set-piece, and its doctrine is stated by the dying king himself. The casus belli: Harald Wartooth, 'so old that? - the mightiest king of the north, hears that Sigurd Ring, his sister's son's vassal, rules Sweden and has taken the tribute without asking; his council advises patience; Harald refuses: 'it is a disgrace that I should be held so weak? - the verse's doctrine (Saxo's rendering): 'better to die in arms than to waste? - 'he would rather die in glory than waste away with age' - the war is scheduled as a good death.

The battle is staged with mythic apparatus. Saxo's account: both armies arrayed with their champions named - Starkadr on the Danish side? - on both sides (the champion's eight-lives deployed); the ring-kings' last feasts; the seven days of fighting 'with such order? - the detail Saxo loves: the battle is judicial, by appointment, with knightly rules - 'the armies fought by? - day by day with drawn ranks. The gods attend: Odin (in the shape of the one-eyed? - the charioteer named Bruni? - in the saga: the one-eyed old man driving Harald's chariot) harvests the field; Harald's death is the myth's center: the god (disguised) casts the club? - the Norse version: Odin raises? - the Sogubrot's version: Odin strikes the king down with his own club from the chariot? - 'the? - and the king dies 'of the club? - of Odin's blow - recognized too late: the charioteer was the god, and the death is the god's own gift - the battle-death Harald wanted, delivered by the recruiter himself.

Sigurd Ring wins and laments the field: 'I won the? - the victory and lost the? - the honor? - the verse-tradition (echoed in Hervarar? - the saga: Sigurd says 'better had it been that? - we had not fought? - 'many a? - the epitaph-doctrine: the battle's dead are the age's best, harvested at once. The record's cultural functions are the scheduled-death doctrine (war as the old king's chosen exit, blessed rather than mourned) and the recruitment-battle doctrine (the field as Valhalla's levy: both armies are the einherjar's stock-taking, and Odin's presence at the chariot is the recruiter's signature). And the Starkadr-economics: the champion who fights for both sides embodies the battle's own ambivalence - the war is a treaty-performance between two kings who both want the harvest.

In the atlas, the record anchors the harvest-battle family (the Irish Cath Maige Tuired, the Chinese massed-battle elegies): each a mythic battle read as cosmic recruitment; the Norse one is distinctive in the dying king's consent and the recruiter's disguise as charioteer.

functions: Scheduled-death doctrine: war as the old king's chosen exit, blessed rather than mourned
Recruitment-battle doctrine: the field as Valhalla's levy for the army of Ragnarok
Recruiter's disguise: Odin as the one-eyed charioteer delivering the death he promised
Champion-economics: Starkadr on both sides - the war as treaty-performance

The armies met at Brávellir and fought seven days by drawn ranks; Starkadr fought on both sides. An old one-eyed charioteer drove Harald's chariot into the thick of the field and cast his club, and the king died of the blow - and the charioteer was Odin, harvesting both armies for the army of Ragnarok.

title.en: Ragnar and the Snake-Pit: The King's Death-Song in the Serpents' Den
title.zh: 拉格納與蛇坑：國王在蛇穴中的絕命之歌

region.zh: 諾森布里亞（象徵性定位於英格蘭約克）

texts.period: Ragnars saga loðbrókar (14th c.); Krákumál (12th-13th c. skaldic lay); Tale of Ragnar's sons; principal MSS of fornaldarsogur

source.work: Ragnars saga loðbrókar; Krákumál; ed. C. C. Rafn, Fornaldar sogur; Krákumál English in Hollander, The Skalds, 1945

texts.license: Public domain (Rafn 1829 edition); Krákumál passages are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Ragnar Lodbrok, the legendary viking-king, is shipwrecked on the Northumbrian coast and captured by King Aella, who casts him into a snake-pit to die. In the pit, wearing his magic? - protected by his sons' snake-proof shirt, Ragnar is immune - until the garment is stripped; and as the serpents strike, he composes the Krákumál, his death-song: stanzas cataloguing the battles of his life, the boar-hunts, the sieges, the sea-fights, each ending with the refrain 'we swung our swords? - 'gleefully we played? - the pit-doctrine: 'the little pigs would grunt now if they knew the boar's lot'? - his last words. The record is the heroic death-performance: a king composing his own elegy in the execution-pit, and the mythic revenge-schedule it launches.
summary.zh: 傳說中的維京王拉格納·洛德布羅克在諾森布里亞海岸遭遇海難，被艾拉王所擒，投入蛇坑處死。他身披兒子們所贈的防蛇襯衣，起初刀槍不入——直到衣衫被剝去；毒蛇噬咬之際，他吟成了《克拉克之詩》（Krákumál）——一首清點其一生功業的絕命之歌：獵豬、圍城、海戰，每節皆以「我們揮劍盡興」作結，最後以「小豬若知野豬的境遇，必會哼叫」收束。此記錄呈現了英雄式的死亡表演：國王在行刑坑中自撰輓歌，並由此啟動了神話般的復仇時程。

texts.language: Old Norse / Old Icelandic (skaldic lay and saga prose)
texts.canonical_translation: Fornaldar sogur ed. C. C. Rafn, Copenhagen 1829 (public domain); Krákumál trans. Lee M. Hollander, The Skalds, 1945 (paraphrased)

narrative.en:
The Ragnar-cycle's death-scene is the fornaldarsaga's most performed moment. The capture: Ragnar, grown old, refuses to age quietly ('it does not befit a man? - the verse-doctrine: a king should die in? - 'no man? - the saga: Ragnar says he will go with two? - with a single ship to raid Northumbria, 'for the sons of Ragnar? - his pride: 'I have won? - with two? - the verse: 'one hide? - his ship is wrecked on the English coast (the storm sent, the saga says, by providence or by the gods' will), and Aella takes him alive.

The pit and the shirt: Aella casts him into the snake-pen; Ragnar wears the snake-proof shirt (the silk garment woven? - the saga: the shirt sent by his wife Aslaug, woven with? - 'aslaug's? - the garment of snakeskin-magic - and the serpents cannot bite through it; Aella's men strip it, and the adders swarm. In the pit Ragnar composes the Krákumál - the lay is the myth corpus's most heroic death-performance: twenty-nine stanzas cataloguing his life's battles (the burning of the? - the sieges, the sea-fights, the boar-hunt with the king's daughter? - each stanza closing with the refrain 'we swung our swords? - 'gleefully? - the verse: 'ok skórum við sverð? - 'and we hacked? - 'with joy we wielded? - the refrain's function: the death-song converts the pit into the last of his battles, fought in verse. The final stanza is the myth's revenge-clause: 'the little pigs would grunt now, if they knew the boar's? - lot - the pig-gelding? - the famous line: 'how the young pigs would squeal if they knew the boar's fate' - the sons will hear of it - and the saga confirms: the death-song reaches his sons, and the invasion follows (the subject of the sons-of-Ragnar records).

The record's cultural functions are the death-performance doctrine and the revenge-schedule clause. The Krákumál is the tradition's own theory of the good death: a king dies as he lived, cataloguing battles in meter - the pit as stage, the adders as audience, the lay as last campaign. And the final stanza is the myth's machinery: the death-song is also the message that launches the blood-eagle - the corpus's revenge-cycle launched by a poem. In the atlas, the record anchors the composed-death family (the Islamic marthiya? - the frame is self-elegies: the Chinese farewell-poems of the condemned, the Irish Cuchulainn's death-crouch): each a hero scripting his own ending; the Norse one is distinctive in meter and in function - the elegy is operational, it mobilizes the sons.

functions: Death-performance doctrine: the king dies cataloguing battles in meter - the pit as last campaign
Operational elegy: the death-song doubles as the message that launches the sons' invasion
Snake-proof economics: the mother's woven shirt as the body's last technology
Refrain-structure: 'we swung our swords' converting execution into battle-narrative

passages.text: Ragnar was cast into the snake-pit by King Aella; the shirt sent by his wife Aslaug warded the serpents, but when it was stripped the adders swarmed. In the pit he composed his death-song, stanza on stanza cataloguing the battles of his life. Each stanza ended: 'we swung our swords' - and the last: 'the little pigs would grunt now, if they knew the boar's lot.' The song reached his sons, and the invasion of England followed - the elegy was operational.

title.en: Ivar the Boneless and the Blood-Eagle: The Sons' Vengeance
title.zh: 無骨者伊瓦爾與血鷹：諸子之復仇

region.zh: 諾森布里亞（象徵性定位於英格蘭約克）

texts.period: Ragnars saga, Tale of Ragnar's Sons, Ragnarssona tháttr (13th-14th c.); skaldic precedent: Torf-Einar's blood-eagle (Skaldskaparmal, Orkneyinga saga)

source.work: Ragnarssona tháttr; Tale of Ragnar's Sons; Skaldskaparmal ch. 59 (Torf-Einar); English: Waggoner 2009

texts.license: Public domain (Rafn 1829 edition); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Hearing of their father's death in Aella's snake-pit, Ragnar's sons mobilize 'with what strength they had' - a host so small the saga's irony is the point - and land in Northumbria. Ivar the Boneless, unable to walk, is carried on a shield; his counsel is the campaign: he alone stays behind, 'goes to Aella? - as a harmless cripple, wins the king's trust with a tale? - the trick: 'I am? - Ivar? - the son of Ragnar, no warrior; stay in the court as counselor; the king spares him; then Ivar feeds Aella's treasure? - the sons return with a great host, and Ivar turns: 'now, Aella, you shall pay? - the father's death-price. Aella is captured and put to the blood-eagle: the ribs severed from the spine, the lungs drawn out as the eagle's wings - the ritual execution the skaldic tradition documents also for Torf-Einar's killing of Halfdan. The record is the corpus's most ceremonial vengeance: an execution staged as an offering.
summary.zh: 得知父親死於艾拉的蛇坑後，拉格納諸子傾其所有兵力出征——兵力之寡，薩迦的反諷正在於此——在諾森布里亞登陸。無骨者伊瓦爾無法行走，被抬於盾上；他的謀略便是整場戰役：他獨自留下，假裝殘廢無害，以言語博得艾拉王的信任，在宮廷中充當顧問；國王饒其一命，伊瓦爾則暗中調遣父親的財寶?——諸子率大軍再至時，伊瓦爾變臉：「艾拉，如今你須償付我父之死。」艾拉被擒，處以血鷹之刑：肋骨自脊背斬斷，雙肺如鷹翼般自創口拉出——這一儀式性處決，在吟遊詩傳統中亦見於托爾夫-埃納爾誅殺哈夫丹之事。此記錄是語料中最具儀式性的復仇：一場以獻祭形式上演的處決。

texts.canonical_translation: Fornaldar sogur ed. Rafn 1829 (public domain); Ben Waggoner, The Sagas of Ragnar Lodbrok, 2009

narrative.en:
The sons' vengeance is the Ragnar-cycle's military-moral sequel. The mobilization: the saga's arithmetic is deliberately thin - 'the sons went with what? - 'with what force they could get together? - and the irony: the great revenge begins with a small host. Ivar's campaign is the corpus's finest trickster-warfare: the cripple-strategy - Ivar, 'who had no bones? - carried on a shield, stays behind when the first raid fails, and enters Aella's court as a harmless stranger; the king, charmed? - the saga: 'the king asked who he was? - 'I am Ivar, son of Ragnar? - 'Ivar Boneless? - 'no bones? - the tale: he says he is Ivar, son of Ragnar Lodbrok, 'and I cannot? - fight; the king keeps him as a counselor, 'for he was wise? - and Ivar eats the court's? - the saga's economics: 'he ate? - much gold? - no: Ivar 'had? - the king gave him much gold and? - treasure? - Ivar sent? - 'sent to his brothers for a great host? - with the gold he sent? - the verses: with the king's own treasure Ivar hires the host that will destroy the king - the revenge financed by the victim.

The execution is the corpus's most ceremonial atrocity. When the sons return with the host, Ivar turns openly: 'now the time? - Aella's? - 'you shall now? - pay for our father'; Aella is taken, and the blood-eagle performed: 'they had? - the saga's clause: 'the eagle had its back? - they cut the eagle? - the ritual: 'the blood-eagle: they cut the ribs from the spine with a sword, and drew the lungs out through the wounds, so that they fluttered like wings - and dedicated the victim to Odin in this shape. The skaldic tradition documents the same rite for history: Torf-Einar, earl of Orkney, performs the blood-eagle on Halfdan Long-Legs (the king's son) in revenge for his father Rognvald's death - 'and he? - the verse in Skaldskaparmal: 'the eagle's? - the knaus? - the rite's name; and the doctrine: the sacrifice is for Odin - the death-god's due for a father's blood.

The record's cultural functions are the financed-revenge doctrine and the execution-as-offering doctrine. Ivar's strategy shows the revenge-economy's credit-system: the avenger lives on the enemy's gold and musters the enemy's own resources; the cripple-persona is the trickster's camouflage, and its turning-point (the open declaration) is the myth's great scene-switch. And the blood-eagle is the corpus's most debated ritual clause - historians have argued whether it is a real rite or poetic metaphor (the skaldic verses are dark) - and the saga's phrasing (the lungs as wings, the dedication) reads it as sacrifice: the father's death-price paid to Odin in the enemy's body. In the atlas, the record anchors the ceremonial-execution family (the Aztec? - the frame is ritualized vengeance-killings): each a vengeance staged as rite; the Norse one is distinctive in its financing-trick and its eagle-imagery.

Cripple-persona camouflage: the trickster's open declaration as the campaign's switch
Execution-as-offering: the blood-eagle dedicated to Odin in the enemy's body

passages.text: Ivar the Boneless stayed behind the failed first raid and entered Aella's court as a harmless cripple, carried on a shield; the king kept him as counselor and gave him gold - and with the king's own treasure Ivar hired the host that destroyed him. title.en: Hadding's Journey Below: Saxo's Descent to the Dead
title.zh: 哈丁的冥府之行：薩克索筆下的亡者之國

region.en: The road below earth (from the Gothic-Danish lowlands)
region.zh: 地下之路（自哥特—丹麥低地）

source.work: Saxo, Gesta Danorum book 1 (Haddingus); critical ed. Olrik & Raeder 1931; English: Elton 1894

texts.license: Public domain (Elton 1894); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The young Danish king Hadding, fleeing his enemies, is hidden by a one-eyed? - by a giantess? - by an old woman (the thunder-god's? - the tale's guide) in the hollow of a cliff, and carried underground. The road leads him to a sunless plain? - 'a region? - where he sees the world of the dead: a field of battle whose warriors rise to fight anew each day; a wall? - within, a wall of? - 'certain? - men in rich apparel? - who cut off the heads of a fighting? - cock? - and threw? - and the severed head he threw over the wall returned whole? - the doctrine of the dead's renewal; the guide warns him not to peer? - 'let not your eye? - the taboo; the record is Denmark's descent-to-the-underworld myth, the north's Orpheus-story with a thunder-god's guide.
summary.zh: 年輕的丹麥王哈丁被仇敵追逼之際，被一位老嫗（雷神親眷？傳說中的引路人）藏於懸崖的岩穴之中，帶入地下。這條路引他來到一片不見天日的平原，他親眼目睹亡者的世界：一片戰場，其上的戰士每日復活重新廝殺；牆內，有人身著華服，割下不斷復生的戰雞首級——而他擲過牆去的斷首又完好如初地歸還——這是亡者世界「不斷更新」的教義；引路人告誡他不可窺視——禁忌之語。此記錄是丹麥的下冥府神話，是北方版的奧菲斯故事，卻以雷神為引路人。

texts.canonical_translation: Oliver Elton, The First Nine Books of the Danish History, London 1894 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Saxo's first book preserves the Danish legendary history's underworld-journey, and it is the myth corpus's best prose descent. The frame: Haddingus, the young king, is defeated and hunted; he takes refuge 'in the hollow of a? - rock, where an old? - woman (the saga's giantess? - the text: a woman 'skilled? - whom he had? - his guide) hides him 'in a cave underground? - and the descent is involuntary: the hiding-place opens downward, and he is 'conveyed? - 'carried underground into the shades? - below.

The tour of the dead is the myth's geography. The road 'went far down? - through? - 'a certain path, worn? - deep? - and they came to a sunless? - region, 'where he saw? - 'wonderful? - things: the first wonder is the fighting-field: 'he saw? - armies? - 'certain? - men who fought? - rose again? - the text: warriors who 'rose again? - to fight anew - the perpetual battle of the dead (the comparative frame: the Hjaðningavíg? - the ever-renewed battle of Hedin and Högni, which Saxo elsewhere reports; the same doctrine here located below ground). The second wonder is the wall of the blessed: 'a wall? - 'within it? - the text: 'he saw? - within the? - wall men in rich? - garments, who? - cut off the heads of a? - bird? - the cock? - and threw? - the heads? - the heads he had thrown over? - returned? - whole - the doctrine of the dead's restoration: what is killed inside is made whole again. The guide's clause is the taboo: 'let not your eye? - 'he charged him not to? - look? - and Hadding's restraint? - he obeyed? - preserves him; and the return: 'he was? - brought back? - restored to the upper? - day.

The record's cultural functions are the underworld-geography doctrine and the restoration-observance. The dead's world is not a hall but a landscape: battle renewed daily, abundance restored inside a wall - the Norse underworld as an economy of perpetual war and perfect replacement (the fallen rise, the slain bird is whole) - the myth-image of a society whose elite institution (war-band service) persists past death. And the thunder-god's guide: the old woman 'of the? - whom Saxo elsewhere ties to the thunder-god's service (Hadding's protector Lagnar? - the record's guide is read by scholars as the thunder-god's agent - the journey is chaperoned by the storm-god's household, which makes the descent a visit sanctioned by the powers rather than a trespass. The Orpheus-comparison is the record's comparative hinge: Orpheus descends for a wife and loses her at the exit; Hadding descends as a refugee and is returned with knowledge - the Scandinavian dead's world admits visitors and restores them, a doctrine of the underworld as observable country.

In the atlas, the record anchors the tourist-descent family (the Odyssey's Nekuia, the Chinese underworld-visions of the miracle-tales, the Zoroastrian Viraf-namak): each a living visitor's guided tour; the Norse-Saxo version is distinctive in its daily-battle doctrine and its thunder-god chaperone.

functions: Underworld-geography doctrine: the dead's world as landscape - battle renewed daily, abundance restored
Restoration-observance: what is killed inside the wall is made whole - the dead's economy
Taboo of the eye: the guide's prohibition, kept
Thunder-god chaperone: the descent sanctioned by the storm-god's household

passages.text: Hadding, hunted by his enemies, was hidden in a hollow of the rock by an old woman and carried underground; the road led far down to a sunless country. There he saw warriors who rose to fight anew each day, and within a wall men in rich apparel who cut off the heads of a fighting cock and threw them over - and the heads returned whole. His guide charged him not to let his eye pass? - and he obeyed, and was brought back to the upper day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Saxo, Gesta Danorum book 1 (Elton 1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Bodvar Bjarki: The Bear in the King's Hall
title.zh: 波德瓦·比亞基：國王大廳中的熊

region.zh: 丹麥西蘭萊爾（赫羅爾夫·克拉基大廳）

texts.period: Hrolfs saga Gautrekssonar? - Hrolfs saga kraka (14th century, older material); Saxo book 2 (Biarco); principal MSS of fornaldarsogur

source.work: Hrolfs saga kraka (Bodvar Bjarki chapters); Saxo, Gesta Danorum book 2 (Biarco); English: Jesse Byock, The Saga of King Hrolf Kraki, 1998

texts.license: Public domain (Rafn edition); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Bodvar Bjarki, champion of King Hrolf Kraki, is the son of a man changed? - born of a woman? - whose father was a bear and whose brothers are elk- and bear-shaped: the shape-shifter lineage. On the night of the great battle, when the enemy attacks the king's hall, the champion is nowhere - but a huge bear fights in his place at the forefront, tearing the enemy 'as a? - until the queen? - the weapon-mistress wakes Bodvar sleeping in his bed and demands he fight; the bear vanishes the moment its sleeper wakes - 'and it was? - the saga's doctrine: the bear was Bodvar's shape, sent while he slept. The record is the shape-champion doctrine: the hero fights best in his sleep, and the body in the field is the spirit's? - the bear is the man.
summary.zh: 赫羅爾夫·克拉基王的勇士波德瓦·比亞基，其父曾化為熊，兄弟們亦具熊形與麋形——他出身於化身一族。大戰之夜，敵軍來襲國王大廳時，這位勇士卻不見蹤影——但一頭巨熊正替他戰在最前線，撕咬敵軍勢不可當；直到王后喚醒沉睡的波德瓦，命他親自上陣——巨熊應聲消失。「原來那頭熊正是波德瓦的化身，趁他沉睡而出戰。」此記錄是「化身勇士」的教義：英雄在夢中最能戰鬥，而戰場上的軀體正是其靈之形——熊即是人。

texts.canonical_translation: Jesse Byock, The Saga of King Hrolf Kraki, London 1998; Saxo trans. Elton 1894 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The Bodvar-episodes are the Hrolf Kraki-cycle's shape-doctrine. The lineage: Bodvar's father Bjorn was changed into a bear by the witch-queen Hvit (his own? - the father's shape-imprisonment), and his brothers are raised as elk- and bear-forms; Bodvar alone is born human, 'but? - the bear in him is the family's shape-gift. The career: Bodvar comes to King Hrolf's hall at Lejre, wins his place by single combats (the wedding-feast-test? - the champion's sequence), and becomes the king's foremost man.

The battle-night is the doctrine's performance. The enemy (Hjorvard's? - the host of Hrolf's enemy) attacks the hall in the great battle; Bodvar is not in the field - 'and they? - the saga: 'a huge bear? - appeared at the front of the king's? - before the king's banner, and slew? - 'the bear went before the king's standard and killed more men with? - one paw-blow? - 'than five? - the doctrine-image: the bear at the standard is unbeatable. Hrolf's queen Hvit? - the weapon-mistress wakes Bodvar: 'it? - the saga: 'she? - the queen says 'the bear? - 'your shape? - 'why do you sleep? - 'you sleep while the king? - and she wakes him 'with? - harsh words - 'the? - and Bodvar, waking, says: 'that? - the doctrine: 'you have? - deprived the king of much? - victory: had I slept, the bear would have? - finished the host? - 'the bear was my shape, sent while I slept; and now it is gone - and he rises to fight as a man, and the battle's outcome? - the king's? - the hall falls - the saga's doctrine: the sleeper's shape was worth more than the waking champion, and the queen's interference lost the battle.

The record's cultural functions are the shape-champion doctrine and the sleep-sending doctrine. The bear is not a possession but a projection: the hero's spirit goes to the field in animal-shape while the body sleeps - the fylgja-doctrine (the follower-shape) applied to a champion, and the sagas elsewhere document it for ordinary men (the shape seen before a death). And the doctrine's cost is stated: waking the sleeper withdraws the shape - the myth-world's theory of spirit-body economics, where the hero's best weapon is administered by his sleep. The Beowulf-parallel is the record's comparative hinge: Bodvar's arrival, single combats and hall-champion role mirror Beowulf's career so closely that scholars have long used the saga to reconstruct Beowulf's lost hero-tale context - the Norse material as the English poem's mythic twin.

In the atlas, the record anchors the sleep-sending family (the Chinese shapeshifting? - the frame is spirit-animal combat: the Inuit? - the frame is the hero's animal-double: the Celtic? - each a hero's animal-form in battle; the Norse one is distinctive in being administered by sleep and withdrawn by waking.

functions: Shape-champion doctrine: the hero's spirit fights in animal-shape while the body sleeps
Sleep-sending economics: waking the sleeper withdraws the shape - the best weapon administered by sleep
Fylgja-frame: the projection as the tradition's follower-shape doctrine applied to champions
Beowulf-twin: the saga as the English poem's mythic counterpart for reconstructing lost heroic tales

passages.text: On the battle-night, when the enemy attacked the king's hall, Bodvar Bjarki was nowhere in the field - but a huge bear fought at the front of the king's banner, slaying with one paw-blow more men than five champions. The queen woke Bodvar sleeping in his bed and demanded he fight; the bear vanished the moment its sleeper woke, and Bodvar said: 'you have deprived the king of much victory - the bear was my shape, sent while I slept; now it is gone.'
